statement: Three friends each choose one of 5 different clubs to join. They do not have to choose different clubs. In how many different ways can the three choices turn out?

choices.misconception: I counted the ways to pick 3 of the 5 clubs, as if the friends had to choose different clubs and it did not matter who chose which.
I multiplied the 3 friends by the 5 clubs instead of multiplying the choices of the three friends.
I made the friends choose different clubs, 5 × 4 × 3, but they are allowed to join the same club.
I let each of the 5 clubs choose one of the 3 friends, 3 to the power 5, but it is the friends who each make one choice.

hints: Who is making a choice, and how many options does each have?
Each friend makes one independent choice, and the three choices happen together, so multiply the numbers of options. Check which way round the power goes.
Each of the 3 friends has 5 options, whatever the others choose.

solutions.reliable: The first friend has 5 options, the second also has 5 (repeats are allowed), and so does the third. The choices happen together, so the total is $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$. The transferable idea: in the multiplication principle, multiply over the things that make the choices; here each friend makes one choice from 5, giving $5^3$, not $3^5$.

whyOnTest: The multiplication principle is easy to state but easy to turn upside down; the traps are the wrong power and forbidding repeats.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
